reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Usually an incidental radiographic finding of numerous small, symmetrical, round or oval sclerotic foci clustered in the epiphyses and metaphyses of long bones and in the pelvis, carpus and tarsus
The individual is typically asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they are mild joint aches rather than a destructive process
Caused by loss-of-function variants in LEMD3, encoding an inner nuclear membrane protein that antagonises BMP and TGF-beta signalling, leading to focal islands of dense trabecular bone
Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance, so unaffected-appearing relatives may still carry the variant
Bone scintigraphy characteristically shows no increased uptake in the sclerotic foci, an important feature distinguishing it from osteoblastic metastases
When cutaneous connective-tissue naevi (elastomas or collagenomas) coexist with the spotty bone lesions, the combined disorder is termed Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome
Management is generally reassurance and avoidance of unnecessary intervention once the benign nature is confirmed
reference.pathophysiology: Osteopoikilosis arises from heterozygous loss-of-function variants in LEMD3, whose protein product resides in the inner nuclear membrane and normally dampens bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor-beta signalling. Reduced antagonism tips the balance towards osteoblastic activity in discrete foci, producing scattered islands of compact lamellar bone within the spongiosa. These enostosis-like foci concentrate near the ends of long bones and around the pelvis and short tubular bones, remain metabolically quiet, and do not disturb the overall bone architecture, explaining the asymptomatic incidental presentation and the absence of scintigraphic uptake.
additionalDifferentials: Osteoblastic (sclerotic) skeletal metastases, particularly from prostate or breast carcinoma
Tuberous sclerosis with sclerotic bone islands
Melorheostosis (which can coexist within the LEMD3 spectrum)
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs or skeletal survey demonstrating the characteristic symmetrical sclerotic foci
Bone scintigraphy to confirm absent tracer uptake and help exclude metastatic disease
Cross-sectional imaging where distinction from metastasis remains uncertain
Skin examination and, if lesions are present, biopsy for connective-tissue naevi (Buschke-Ollendorff overlap)
LEMD3 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and inform family counselling
Family history review and consideration of imaging in first-degree relatives
redFlags: New focal bone pain or a lesion showing increasing size, cortical destruction or scintigraphic uptake, suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as metastasis
Unexplained weight loss or a known primary malignancy raising concern for osteoblastic metastases mimicking the foci
Progressive limb pain or contracture suggesting associated melorheostosis
reference.prognosis: The skeletal condition is benign and does not shorten life or cause meaningful disability; the main risk is diagnostic confusion with malignancy leading to unnecessary investigation, and prognosis is excellent once the diagnosis is recognised.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the sclerotic foci as osteoblastic metastases and initiating an unnecessary oncological workup
Overlooking coexisting cutaneous connective-tissue naevi that would establish Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome
Failing to counsel relatives despite the autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance
Attributing incidental joint symptoms wholly to the bone foci rather than considering another cause
